name: Aphids
symptoms: Curled, distorted, or yellowing leaves
Sticky honeydew coating on leaves and stems
Sooty mold growing on the honeydew
Stunted new growth and deformed buds
Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides
lifecycle: Egg — overwinters on host plant in cold climates
Nymph — 4 instars over 7-10 days to maturity
Adult — winged females disperse in summer; wingless females reproduce asexually (parthenogenesis)
10-30 generations per year depending on climate
One female can produce 80+ offspring without mating
treatmentOrganic: Spray strong jet of water to dislodge — repeat every 2 days
Apply insecticidal soap to infested foliage every 5-7 days
Release ladybugs, lacewings, or parasitic wasps
Spray neem oil weekly until populations crash
Dust diatomaceous earth on dry foliage as a barrier
treatmentChemical: Imidacloprid systemic for severe ornamental infestations
prevention: Companion plant with marigolds, garlic, chives, and nasturtiums
Encourage beneficial insects with diverse flowering plants
Avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen (lush growth attracts aphids)
Inspect new plants before introducing them
Use reflective mulch to confuse winged aphids

name: Armyworm
symptoms: Ragged holes chewed in leaves, often overnight
Skeletonised leaves with only veins remaining
Plants stripped down to the stalk in severe outbreaks
Frass (dark pellets) on leaves and at the plant base
Caterpillars feed at night and hide under debris by day
lifecycle: Egg — laid in clusters of 50-200 on leaves or grasses
Larva — 6 instars over 14-21 days; this is the damaging stage
Pupa — pupates in the soil for 7-14 days
Adult moth — lives 9-14 days and lays up to 1,500 eggs
3-6 generations per year, migrates over long distances
treatmentOrganic: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt) at dusk every 5-7 days
Hand-pick larvae in the early morning or after dark
Apply spinosad spray for advanced infestations
Release Trichogramma egg parasitoid wasps
Apply nematode (Steinernema carpocapsae) drench to the soil
treatmentChemical: Chlorantraniliprole at first sign of damage
Emamectin benzoate for resistant fall armyworm
Rotate insecticide classes to prevent resistance
prevention: Pheromone traps to monitor adult moth flights
Encourage natural enemies — birds, ground beetles, parasitic wasps
Maintain weed-free field borders that harbour egg-laying moths
Plant trap crops (e.g. napier grass border for maize)
Scout fields weekly during peak season
Till crop residue after harvest to expose pupae

name: Whitefly
symptoms: Tiny white moth-like insects fly up when foliage is disturbed
Yellowing, mottled, or curling leaves
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold growth
Stunted plants and reduced yields
Virus transmission (e.g. tomato yellow leaf curl, cassava mosaic)
lifecycle: Egg — laid on leaf undersides, hatches in 5-10 days
Nymph — 4 instars over 2-4 weeks, sessile after first instar
Pupa — non-feeding stage inside the final nymph skin
Adult — lives 30-60 days and lays 200-400 eggs
Continuous breeding in warm climates and greenhouses
treatmentOrganic: Hang yellow sticky traps near affected plants
Spray insecticidal soap on leaf undersides every 5-7 days
Apply neem oil at dusk every 7-10 days
Release Encarsia formosa parasitoid wasps in greenhouses
Vacuum adults from foliage in the early morning while sluggish
treatmentChemical: Pyriproxyfen insect growth regulator on nymphs
Spiromesifen for both nymphs and eggs
prevention: Use reflective silver mulch to repel adults
Install fine insect-mesh on greenhouse vents
Inspect transplants thoroughly before bringing them home
Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves
Avoid planting whitefly-magnet hosts (e.g. poinsettia) near vegetables
Rotate to non-host crops in heavily infested fields

name: Thrips
symptoms: Silvery or bronze streaks on leaves and petals
Black specks of frass on damaged surfaces
Distorted growth and deformed flowers
Tomato spotted wilt virus transmission
Slender 1-2 mm insects visible with a hand lens
lifecycle: Egg — inserted into plant tissue, hatches in 3-5 days
Larva — 2 instars over 7-14 days on leaves and flowers
Pupa — pre-pupal and pupal stages in the soil or leaf litter
Adult — lives 30-45 days and lays 80+ eggs
Up to 15 generations per year in warm climates
treatmentOrganic: Hang blue sticky traps near affected plants
Spray spinosad every 7 days during outbreaks
Apply insecticidal soap to all leaf surfaces
Release predatory mites (Amblyseius cucumeris)
Drench soil with beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae)
treatmentChemical: Methomyl for emergency knockdown (highly toxic — last resort)
prevention: Use insect-mesh screens on greenhouses (mesh < 0.2 mm)
Avoid planting near grassy field margins
Remove weeds that host thrips year-round
Mulch with reflective material to deter flight
Quarantine new ornamentals for 2 weeks before introducing

name: Spider Mites
symptoms: Fine speckling or stippling on upper leaf surfaces
Fine silken webbing on leaf undersides and between stems
Bronzed, dusty, or pale appearance on heavily infested leaves
Leaf drop and stunted growth in severe cases
Tiny (< 0.5 mm) red, yellow, or green mites visible with a hand lens
lifecycle: Egg — laid singly on leaf undersides, hatches in 3 days at 26 °C
Larva — 6-legged, feeds for 1-2 days
Protonymph + deutonymph — 8-legged immatures over 4-5 days
Adult — lives 2-4 weeks, female lays 100+ eggs
Complete life cycle in 5-20 days; many generations per season
treatmentOrganic: Spray strong jet of water on leaf undersides every 2-3 days
Apply insecticidal soap weekly to all foliage surfaces
Spray horticultural oil to smother eggs and adults
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
Increase humidity around houseplants — mites prefer dry conditions
treatmentChemical: Avoid pyrethroids — they kill predatory mites worse than spider mites
prevention: Maintain adequate watering and humidity
Mist houseplant foliage regularly
Avoid dusty conditions that protect mites from predators
Inspect new plants under leaves for early webbing
Encourage native predators by reducing broad-spectrum spray use

name: Scale
symptoms: Small bumpy oval discs (1-5 mm) attached to stems and leaves
Yellow chlorotic spots beneath the scale insect
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on soft scale infestations
Branch dieback and overall plant decline
Heavily infested plants may shed leaves prematurely
lifecycle: Egg — laid under the female scale cover
Crawler — mobile newly-hatched stage; this is when scale is vulnerable
Settled nymph — inserts mouthparts and forms its protective covering
Adult female — lays 100-1000 eggs under her shell; legless and immobile
1-3 generations per year depending on species and climate
treatmentOrganic: Scrape scale off small infestations with a soft brush
Spray dormant horticultural oil on woody hosts in late winter
Apply summer-weight oil to active crawlers in spring/summer
Dab individual scales with rubbing alcohol on a cotton swab
Encourage parasitic wasps (Aphytis, Encarsia) and ladybirds
treatmentChemical: Imidacloprid soil drench for systemic ornamental control
prevention: Inspect new plants for scale before bringing them home
Prune dense interior growth to expose hidden scales
Avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen
Monitor with sticky tape wrapped around stems to catch crawlers
Maintain healthy plant vigor — stressed plants attract scale

name: Mealybugs
symptoms: White cottony or waxy masses on stems, leaf joints, and roots
Yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on affected plants
Distorted new growth and dropping leaves
Heavy infestations cling to leaf undersides in cottony clusters
lifecycle: Egg — laid in cottony egg sacs, hatches in 7-10 days
Crawler — 1st instar nymphs disperse to feeding sites
Nymph — 3 instars over 6-10 weeks (longer for males)
Adult female — lives 2-3 months, lays 300-600 eggs
Males have wings and exist briefly to mate; do not feed
Continuous breeding indoors; 2-3 outdoor generations per year
treatmentOrganic: Dab individual mealybugs with 70 % isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab
Wash off colonies with strong water spray weekly
Apply insecticidal soap to all stem joints and undersides
Release Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (mealybug destroyer beetle)
Spray neem oil every 7 days to smother and disrupt growth
treatmentChemical: Acetamiprid for systemic control on ornamentals
Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill mealybug predators
prevention: Quarantine new plants for 3-4 weeks before introducing
Wipe leaves regularly to detect early infestations
Avoid overcrowding plants — mealybugs spread by touch
Keep dust off leaves — encourages mealybugs and discourages predators
Repot houseplants in fresh sterile media every 1-2 years

name: Beetles
symptoms: Holes chewed in leaves, sometimes skeletonising the leaf
Damaged flowers and developing fruit
Visible adult beetles feeding in groups
Larvae (grubs) damaging roots in the soil
Wilting plants where root feeding is heavy
lifecycle: Egg — laid in soil or on host foliage
Larva (grub) — 3 instars over weeks to months, feeds on roots
Pupa — pupates in soil chamber for 2-3 weeks
Adult — flies, feeds, and mates for several weeks
1 generation per year for most species (e.g. Japanese beetle, cucumber beetle)
treatmentOrganic: Hand-pick adults in the early morning and drown in soapy water
Apply neem oil weekly to deter feeding and disrupt eggs
Spray pyrethrin or spinosad for active infestations
Apply beneficial nematodes (Heterorhabditis) to soil for grubs
Use floating row covers until flowering for cucurbits
treatmentChemical: Carbaryl as a broad-spectrum knockdown on adults
prevention: Companion plant with garlic, chives, and tansy
Use kaolin clay foliar coating to deter feeding
Hand-tilling exposes pupae to birds and weather
Avoid drought-stressing plants — stressed plants attract beetles
Maintain healthy lawn to reduce grub habitat
Use pheromone traps only at field perimeters (they can attract more beetles)
